metadata.title: What the Baseline Found
metadata.note: Mycroft patent intelligence progress video 12. Real session: labeled 50 independent claims from 16 patents by hand (46 narrow / 4 broad; 50 defensive), ran eval_classifier.py baseline once (50 calls to claude-sonnet-5, cost upper bound $0.32; actual not recorded). Results over 50 claims: breadth acc 0.66, kappa 0.08 (majority baseline 0.92); posture acc 0.60, kappa 0.00 (majority baseline 1.00); no collapse; 11 broad/offensive predictions, 10 of them labeled narrow. Three claims on US-11766760-B2 refused (stop_reason=refusal; claims 1 and 7 recorded, claim 5 same failure); fixed claim_classifier.py to treat refusal as declined. Commit 3bcf1b1 on nikbearbrown/mycroft. Phase 4 prompt fix not started.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Aishwarya from the Mycroft team. This video covers the first real evaluation of our patent claim classifier: fifty hand-labeled claims, one baseline run, and a result that went the opposite way from what we expected.

output: Fifty hand-labeled claims, one baseline run,
and a result that went the other way.

beats.narration_text: For weeks, the classifier's readings looked narrow and defensive, and we suspected it was stuck on one answer. When we finally measured it against human labels, it wasn't stuck there. It was leaning the other way.

beats.role_note: recap: harness + one $0.92 query (last week); 50 claims from 16 patents labeled by hand (this week)
beats.narration_text: Last week I built the evaluation harness and pulled the test set: one BigQuery query, ninety-two cents, one hundred sixty patents. From those I selected fifty independent claims across sixteen patents, two from each of the eight patent classification sections. This week I labeled all fifty by hand, breadth and posture, with a note on each explaining why.

beats.role_note: baseline run: accuracy vs majority baseline; kappa 0.08 / 0.00
beats.narration_text: Then I ran the classifier on all fifty, for at most thirty-two cents. Breadth accuracy was 0.66, posture accuracy 0.60. Accuracy alone is misleading here. Forty-six of my fifty labels are narrow, so a model that always says narrow would score ninety-two percent. Cohen's kappa corrects for that: 0.08 on breadth and 0.00 on posture, which is barely better than chance.

beats.role_note: 11 broad/offensive predictions, 10 labeled narrow; functional wording read as broad; all-defensive label caveat
beats.narration_text: The surprise is the direction. The classifier called eleven claims broad and offensive, and I had labeled ten of those eleven narrow. Its reasoning kept treating functional wording, like "configured to" or "a protrusion", as broad, while I read the named parts and specific limits as narrow. One caveat: every one of my labels is defensive, so this test set can't measure posture agreement well. That needs offensive and broad examples.

beats.role_note: 3 refusals on one grinding patent; mid-answer refusal broke parser; stop_reason fix; 50/50 scored; prompt fix next
beats.narration_text: Three claims on one patent, a cryogenic grinding process, kept failing. Raising the token limit didn't help. One diagnostic call showed why: the model was refusing partway through its answer, leaving half a JSON reply that the parser couldn't read. The code only handled empty refusals. I fixed it to treat any refusal as declined, and all fifty claims now score. The prompt fix comes next.

Your turn. Before you trust any classifier's accuracy, score a fake model that always gives the most common answer. If your real model can't beat it, accuracy is telling you about your data, not your model.

props.command: claude "score a fake model that always predicts my most common label, and compare it with my classifier's accuracy"

beats.narration_text: What the Baseline Found. Built with Claude, for Humanitarians AI.
